html:
The Catawba are a Native American people of the Piedmont of the Carolinas, along the Catawba River. Their language belongs to the Catawban branch of the wider Siouan family.

They lived in farming towns, growing maize, beans and squash, and were known for their pottery, a craft Catawba potters keep alive today. Spanish expeditions passed near their country in the 1500s, and English traders from Virginia and Carolina reached them in the late 1600s.

In the 1700s the Catawba took in many smaller Piedmont peoples broken by disease and war. They allied with the English colonists and fought raiders from the north, among them the Iroquois and the Shawnee, and they were long rivals of the Cherokee. A smallpox epidemic in 1759 killed perhaps half of them. In 1763 they were given a small reservation in South Carolina. To the north, in Virginia, lived the Tutelo, speakers of another Siouan language. Today the Catawba Indian Nation is federally recognised and based near Rock Hill, South Carolina.
